plain: A sheet of epoxy resin about a hundredth of a millimetre thick, laid over the copper wiring of a chip's base board to insulate it before the next layer of wiring goes on. It comes from the Japanese food company Ajinomoto, which developed it out of its amino acid chemistry.
why: One firm supplies more than 95 percent of it, TSMC names it alongside memory as a limit on AI supply, and Ajinomoto's next new plant will not operate until 2032.

plain: A chip built to do the one kind of arithmetic machine learning needs, multiplying large grids of numbers, far faster than a general-purpose processor can. Nvidia's graphics processors, Google's Tensor Processing Units and Amazon's Trainium are all accelerators.
why: Accelerators are what the whole supply chain is for, and the unit that export licences are granted or refused for.

plain: The steps that assemble several finished chips into one component, sitting side by side or stacked, wired together closely enough to behave like a single larger chip. Ordinary packaging only puts one chip into a protective case with contacts on the bottom.
why: The second tightest bottleneck in the chain after lithography. In 2025 it capped how many AI accelerators could be built; transistor supply did not.

plain: A way of coating a chip roughly one atomic layer at a time. Each pulse of gas sticks to the surface and then stops once the surface is covered, so the film ends up the same thickness on the floor and on the walls of a hole hundreds of times deeper than it is wide.
why: Atomic layer deposition is what makes stacked memory and wrap-around transistors possible, US export rules name it directly, and it is the one tool category where Chinese suppliers still hold under 1 percent of the market.

plain: A one-customer chip, designed for a single job rather than sold on the open market. Google's Tensor Processing Unit and Amazon's Trainium are chips of this kind; an Nvidia part sold to any customer is not.
why: Custom chips are how the largest cloud buyers try to escape Nvidia's pricing, and roughly 95 percent of the co-design work for them runs through just two firms, Broadcom and Marvell.

plain: The machine that connects to a finished chip, feeds it millions of test patterns and checks whether the answers coming back are right. It is the only stage of chip manufacturing that runs electricity through the product.
why: Advantest and Teradyne hold about 80 percent of this market, and changing tester vendor means rebuilding a customer's whole production test environment, so share moves slowly.

plain: A way of joining a packaged chip to a circuit board using a grid of small solder balls across the underside, rather than a row of pins around the edge. Heating the assembly melts every ball at once into a permanent joint.
why: The number and spacing of those balls limit how much current and how many signals can reach a package, which matters when a single AI accelerator draws more than a thousand amps.

plain: The itemised list of every purchased part in a finished product and what each part cost, the way a builder's invoice prices lumber, wiring and fixtures separately.
why: On an AI accelerator the memory line alone is roughly half of manufacturing cost, so the bill of materials shows which suppliers capture the money a buyer spends.

aka: Bureau of Industry and Security, part of the US Department of Commerce
plain: The US government office that decides which technologies may be exported, to whom, and on what conditions. It writes the rules, issues the licences and brings the enforcement cases.
why: Almost every restriction on selling AI chips or chipmaking tools to China is a bureau rule, and the bureau can change a threshold with a Federal Register notice rather than an act of Congress.

plain: Money a company spends on long-lived physical assets such as buildings, machines and servers, as distinct from salaries and other running costs.
why: The five largest cloud companies spent $448 billion of capex in 2025 and have guided higher for 2026, and that is the number every firm in this chain plans against.

plain: One piece of a chip that has been deliberately split into several smaller pieces, each manufactured separately and then wired back together inside a single package. It is a house built from prefabricated rooms rather than poured as one slab.
why: Splitting a design raises yield and lets a firm mix manufacturing processes, but it pushes the difficulty into packaging, which is the more constrained stage.

plain: A step in the supply chain where so few firms or countries can do the work that losing one of them stops everybody. The term comes from Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, which mapped the chip industry segment by segment to find the ones with only one or two suppliers.
why: Chokepoints are where policy gets purchase, and where one sanction or one factory fire reaches the whole industry.

aka: concentration band; Extreme, High, Moderate, Low
plain: The site's four-band judgment of how many firms could credibly supply a stage today, taken at the narrowest step inside it. Extreme means three or fewer, or one firm holding more than half the stage. High means four to six, with the top two taking most of the revenue. Moderate means seven or more, none of them dominant. Low means many, with the scarce input something another industry sells at volume. Where the country-share matrix carries a figure for the segment, the top country's share is a second check, and the supplier count wins when the two disagree.
why: It is the first label on every chokepoint card and sets the bar height in the chain strip. It is a judgment made from supplier counts, not a published measurement.

plain: The buckets US export rules sort the world into, published as supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 740. A:5 and A:6 are close partners; D:1, D:4 and D:5 are the national security, missile technology and arms-embargoed groups; E:1 and E:2 are the most restricted. A country can sit in several at once, and the licence requirement usually turns on which.
why: The licence rule for AI chips is written as country groups, not country names: a licence is needed for D:1, D:4 and D:5 destinations that are not also A:5 or A:6 (15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)). Moving the UAE into A:5 in July 2026 changed its position without naming it in the rule.

plain: TSMC's method for mounting logic chips and memory stacks side by side on a shared slab of silicon, then mounting that slab on a rigid base board. Nearly every high-end AI accelerator is built this way.
why: CoWoS capacity was the practical ceiling on AI accelerator output through 2025, and Nvidia has booked more than half of TSMC's 2026 to 2027 expansion.

plain: The share of controlled US content a foreign-made item may carry before it becomes subject to the EAR. Under 15 CFR 734.4 the general threshold is 25 percent of the item's value, and 10 percent for the most restricted destinations. Above the line the item is caught; below it, it is not.
why: It is the ordinary route out of American jurisdiction, and the reason the foreign direct product rules were written: those rules ignore the percentage altogether. There is no de minimis at all for the advanced-node equipment named in 15 CFR 734.4(a)(3).

plain: The average number of chip-killing flaws per square centimetre of processed wafer. It is a fab's quality score, inferred from how many chips come out working rather than counted directly.
why: Yield falls steeply with die area multiplied by defect density, so on the reticle-sized dies AI chips use, halving defect density nearly doubles the number of saleable parts.

plain: An enforcement order, not a licence policy. Under 15 CFR 764.3 it suspends or revokes a named party's outstanding licences and bars exports, reexports and in-country transfers of any item subject to the EAR to or by that party. There is no application to file. Orders can be issued outright or suspended and later activated.
why: It is the only instrument here that stops trade absolutely. The order activated against ZTE in April 2018 halted most of the company's production within weeks and was terminated 89 days later on settlement (83 FR 17644; 83 FR 34825).

plain: Adding a layer of material to a wafer, either by knocking atoms off a solid target so they land on the surface, or by reacting gases at the surface so a film grows there. It is how the insulators, the wires and the parts of each transistor are built up.
why: Deposition and etch are the volume business of a fab, dominated by Applied Materials, Lam Research and Tokyo Electron, and they are where Chinese toolmakers have gained the most share.

plain: One rectangular chip cut out of a wafer. Hundreds are printed side by side on the same disc and then sliced apart, and each separated rectangle is a die.
why: Cost, yield and export thresholds are all reckoned per die, and AI accelerators use among the largest dies in production, which makes every defect far more expensive.

plain: A computer's main working memory. Each bit is a charge held in a microscopic capacitor that leaks, so the whole chip has to be refreshed thousands of times a second and forgets everything when the power goes off.
why: Three firms make nearly all of it, and their decision to convert capacity to AI memory pushed ordinary memory contract prices up more than 90 percent in a single quarter of 2026.

plain: Chipmaking light with a wavelength of 248 or 193 nanometres, produced by a gas laser. Flooding the gap above the wafer with ultrapure water bends the light further and sharpens the printed image, which is called immersion.
why: Immersion deep ultraviolet is the most advanced lithography China can buy or build, which is where Dutch export licensing draws its line.

plain: The body of US rules that governs the export of commercial and dual-use goods, software and technology, written and enforced by the Bureau of Industry and Security. They run from 15 CFR part 730 to part 774: part 734 sets what they cover, part 742 the licence requirements, part 744 the end-use and end-user controls, part 740 the exceptions and part 764 the penalties.
why: Almost every rule on the board amends these regulations. They are changed by a notice in the Federal Register, not by an act of Congress, which is why a threshold can move in a week.

plain: The label for an item that is subject to the EAR but is not listed anywhere on the Commerce Control List, from 15 CFR 734.3(c). It is a residual category, not a free pass: an EAR99 item still needs a licence if it is going to a listed party or a controlled end use.
why: Most of what a chip plant buys is EAR99. It is the answer to "do I need a licence?" for the great majority of shipments, and the reason the end-user controls in part 744 matter more than the classification for many exporters.

plain: The catalogue number that US export rules assign to a controlled item, rather like a customs tariff code for security-sensitive technology. Number 3A090 covers advanced computing chips and 3B001 covers chipmaking equipment.
why: An item's classification number decides whether it needs a licence, so the technical thresholds written into each number are where the policy bites.

aka: electronic design automation, chip design software
plain: The software that turns a description of what a chip should do into the exact pattern of shapes to be printed on silicon, and proves the result will work before anyone commits money to masks and wafers.
why: Three vendors sell every complete design flow used at the leading edge, which is why cutting China off from them in May 2025 took three letters and no lead time.

plain: Export rules that turn on who the buyer is and what they will do with the item, rather than on what the item is. The same tool can ship freely to one customer and need a licence that will be refused for another.
why: These controls reach past the product to the customer, so a company can lose access because of who owns it or what its site produces, as when US rules were extended to firms majority owned by listed entities.

plain: A published list of foreign companies, institutes and individuals to whom any exporter of an item subject to the EAR needs a licence, not only American suppliers. Each entry states its own licence review policy, so a listing is not one uniform outcome: most carry a presumption of denial; SMIC's is case by case except for items uniquely capable of production at 10 nanometres and below. It is supplement no. 4 to 15 CFR part 744, and the licence requirement is in 15 CFR 744.11.
why: The fastest and bluntest instrument Washington has: it names an organisation rather than a technology. Since September 2025 a listing has reached companies the listed firm half owns, though that extension is stayed to 9 November 2026 (90 FR 50857).

plain: Removing material from a wafer wherever the printed pattern says it should not be, usually by turning a gas into a plasma whose ions and fragments eat one material while leaving the material beside it alone.
why: Stacked memory and wrap-around transistors need holes far deeper than they are wide, which is why US rules control etch tools by hole shape and selectivity rather than by product name.

plain: Chipmaking light at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres, made by dropping molten tin into a vacuum and hitting it with a laser 100,000 times a second to create a plasma hotter than the surface of the sun. Everything absorbs this light, including air and glass, so the machine runs in vacuum and every lens has to be a mirror.
why: One company, ASML, makes every extreme ultraviolet machine on Earth, none has ever been sold to China, and no leading-edge logic or advanced memory process runs without one.

plain: The factory where wafers are processed into chips. It is a cleanroom with a second building's worth of pumps, gas cabinets and water treatment underneath it, and a leading-edge one costs $15 to $25 billion and takes four to six years to build.
why: Fab construction is the slowest and most capital-hungry part of any reshoring plan, which is why subsidy programmes on three continents target it and why the capacity they buy arrives late this decade.

plain: A chip company that designs and sells chips but owns no factory, paying a foundry to manufacture them. Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm and Broadcom all work this way.
why: The fabless model concentrates manufacturing in a handful of foundries, so a designer's supply, cost and geographic exposure are set by a company it does not control.

plain: A transistor whose current-carrying channel is stood on edge like a shark fin so that the controlling gate wraps around three of its sides instead of resting on one. More contact means firmer control and less leakage when the switch is meant to be off.
why: FinFET was the standard transistor shape from roughly 2011 until 2025, and US export rules still use 16 nanometre FinFET production as one threshold for what counts as an advanced fab.

aka: floating point operations per second; a TFLOPS is a trillion of them
plain: A count of how many arithmetic operations on decimal numbers a chip can perform each second, the way horsepower counts an engine's output.
why: The standard unit of AI compute and the basis of export thresholds, but only comparable between chips when the number format behind it is stated.

plain: A US rule that pulls a foreign-made item under American control when two tests are both met: a product scope, meaning the item is the direct product of specified US technology or software, or was made by a plant that is; and a destination or end-user scope, meaning it is going somewhere or to someone the rule names. Both halves are needed. The mechanics are in 15 CFR 734.9.
why: This is what makes US controls extraterritorial. Without it a listed buyer could order the same chip from a supplier outside America; with it, a chip made in Taiwan on American tools for a listed Chinese firm needs a US licence.

plain: A factory business that manufactures chips designed by other companies and promises never to compete with them. TSMC created the model in 1987, and it worked because no single design house sells enough chips to fill a modern fab.
why: TSMC took about 73 percent of foundry revenue in 2026 and nearly all leading-edge production, so one company's capacity plan sets the world's supply of AI chips.

plain: Ways of writing a number using only 8 or 4 bits instead of the 32 a computer traditionally uses. Each number is less precise, but the chip can perform and store far more of them, which suits machine learning better than it would suit accounting.
why: Halving the precision roughly doubles a chip's headline speed, so a performance figure quoted without its number format is meaningless and an export threshold has to say which format it counts.

aka: GAA, nanosheet transistor, RibbonFET at Intel
plain: A transistor in which the controlling gate surrounds the channel that current flows through, rather than touching three sides as a fin does. Surrounding it gives the gate total authority, so the switch still turns fully off as dimensions shrink.
why: Only TSMC, Intel and Samsung can build the 2 nanometre generation's transistor in volume, and it is what drives new demand for atomic layer deposition and sideways etching tools.

plain: A processor originally built to draw video game images by doing thousands of simple calculations simultaneously. That same shape of arithmetic turned out to be what neural networks need, so this chip became the default AI processor.
why: Nvidia holds roughly 70 percent of the AI chip market, and its graphics processors are what most export licences name.

plain: The share of a sale left over after paying what it cost to make the thing, before research, sales and overheads are counted. A 70 percent gross margin means $70 of every $100 of revenue survives manufacturing cost.
why: Gross margin shows where pricing power sits: chip designers, memory makers and inspection-tool vendors keep well over half of each sale, substrate makers about a third, and assembly and test houses under a fifth.

plain: A stack of eight to sixteen memory chips, drilled through with copper columns and mounted a few millimetres from the processor so data reaches the arithmetic units far faster than it could across a motherboard. One such stack moves data roughly thirty times faster than an ordinary memory chip.
why: The most expensive line on an AI accelerator's bill of materials, made by three firms whose entire 2026 output was sold forward before the year began.

aka: high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet, ASML EXE series
plain: The next generation of extreme ultraviolet machine, whose larger mirrors collect light at a wider angle and so resolve smaller features. The wider optics also halve the area printable in one exposure, so a large chip has to be stitched together from two of them.
why: Each machine costs $350 to $400 million, only ten were installed anywhere as of September 2026, and Intel's early adoption against TSMC's delay to 2030 is a real disagreement about where the technology goes.

plain: Joining two chips face to face by pressing their copper pads and the surrounding oxide into direct contact, with no solder in between. Removing the solder lets connections be packed much more tightly and shortens the path heat has to travel out.
why: Taller, cooler memory stacks wait on this step, only two suppliers make the tools, and every slip in their schedule moves the memory roadmap with it.

plain: One of the handful of companies that run data centres at global scale and buy computing hardware by the gigawatt: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and, on most definitions, Oracle.
why: They commit capital years before the hardware exists, and their spending plans are the number every firm in this chain plans against.

plain: A chip company that both designs its products and manufactures them in its own factories. Intel, Samsung and Micron are the main surviving examples.
why: An integrated maker that also rents out factory capacity is competing with its own customers, which is the commercial reason Intel and Samsung struggle to win other firms' flagship designs.

plain: A change in the end use or the end user of an item inside one foreign country, defined at 15 CFR 734.16. Nothing crosses a border: a server legally imported into a country for one customer is transferred when it is resold, or repurposed, for another.
why: It is the leg that catches diversion after landing, and it is why a licence granted for a named Chinese customer does not travel with the hardware. Reexports and in-country transfers of advanced chips to Country Group D:5 keep a presumption of denial even where an export would be read case by case (91 FR 1685).

plain: A slab of silicon carrying wiring but no transistors, used as a miniature circuit board underneath several chips so they can be connected at a density no ordinary board could reach.
why: The interposer's own manufacturing yield, roughly 60 to 70 percent on large ones, is now a real share of an accelerator's cost, and its maximum area caps how much silicon fits in one package.

plain: A letter from BIS to one named company imposing a licence requirement on a specific export, without any rule being published. The authority is written into the regulations themselves, for example 15 CFR 744.23(b), which lets BIS inform a person individually rather than by amending the EAR.
why: It is how the fastest moves are made. The A100 and H100 requirement of August 2022 and the H20 requirement of April 2025 both arrived this way, and the public learned of each from the company's own filing rather than the Federal Register.

plain: A bare chip tested thoroughly enough, before assembly, to be trusted inside something expensive. In an ordinary product a marginal chip costs you one chip; inside a stacked package it can destroy thirty.
why: As packages grow toward ten logic chips and twenty memory stacks, the cost of catching a bad one late pushes testing and burn-in back onto the wafer.

plain: A written carve-out in export rules that lets a shipment go without an individual licence, if it meets stated conditions. The ones that matter for AI chips are NAC and ACA (15 CFR 740.8), HBM (740.25), IEC for allied countries that adopt matching controls (740.24), and RPL for servicing and spare parts (740.10).
why: Exceptions are how a control regime is tuned without rewriting it, and how Washington rewards allies: License Exception IEC, added in September 2024, is open only to countries that have imposed equivalent national controls (89 FR 72926).

plain: The companion to NAC in 15 CFR 740.8, added in December 2024. It authorises the same classes of advanced computing chips worldwide except to Macau and Country Group D:5 entities, without a notification, and allows some transfers within those destinations.
why: The split matters for anyone reading an older table: before December 2024 there was one exception, NAC, and it did both jobs. Confusing the two puts a shipment to Germany through a notification it does not need.

plain: The exception at 15 CFR 740.25 for high bandwidth memory under ECCN 3A090.c with a bandwidth density below 3.3 GB/s per square millimetre. It is open only to exporters headquartered in the United States or in Country Group A:5, and only for stacks bought by the designer of the chip they will be packaged with and shipped straight to the packaging site.
why: It is what keeps a Chinese packaging house in the supply chain for an American or allied designer while the same stacks may not be sold to a Chinese customer. It was written into the December 2024 rule that first controlled HBM (89 FR 96790).

plain: An exception created at 15 CFR 740.29 by the AI Diffusion Rule of January 2025 (90 FR 4544), which would have let limited quantities of advanced chips go to most destinations without a licence. Compliance was not required until 15 May 2025 and the framework was rescinded on 13 May, so it never bound anyone.
why: LPP, AIA and ACM belong to a rule that was published, given an effective date and withdrawn before its compliance date. They are still cited, so they keep an entry.

plain: The exception at 15 CFR 740.8 that lets certain advanced computing chips ship to Macau, to Country Group D:5 and to entities headquartered there, provided the exporter notifies BIS in advance and BIS does not object. It does not cover the data centre parts that meet the 3A090.a parameters, nor the memory in 3A090.c.
why: It is the valve in an otherwise closed door: a notification rather than a licence, for chips below the top band. Since December 2024 the section carries two exceptions, NAC for the restricted destinations and ACA for everywhere else.

plain: Taking heat out of a processor by pumping water through a metal plate bolted directly onto it, instead of blowing air across a finned heatsink. Water carries far more heat per unit of volume, which is the only practical way to cool a rack drawing over a hundred kilowatts.
why: It adds 7 to 10 percent to construction cost but cuts the floor area needed per megawatt by 70 to 85 percent, and an air-cooled data hall cannot host a modern AI rack without a full mechanical rebuild.

plain: Printing a circuit pattern onto a wafer by shining light through a patterned plate and projecting a shrunken image of it onto a light-sensitive coating. It is photography at the scale of nanometres, repeated once for every layer of the chip.
why: The most concentrated stage in the chain, and the resolution a country can reach sets the ceiling on every chip it can make.

plain: The widening gap between how fast a processor can calculate and how fast memory can feed it numbers to work on. Computing speed has been roughly tripling every two years while memory bandwidth has less than doubled over the same period.
why: This gap is why AI accelerators now spend most of their cost and silicon area on memory rather than arithmetic, and why memory suppliers have started earning margins comparable to chip designers.

aka: process control, when grouped with inspection
plain: Measuring what a factory actually built: how wide a printed line came out, how thick a film is, whether this layer sits exactly on top of the last one. Inspection is the related job of hunting for flaws.
why: One firm, KLA, holds about 64 percent of this market, and a sanctioned fab that obtains other tools on the grey market still cannot work out why its yield is low.

aka: double patterning, quadruple patterning, self-aligned quadruple patterning
plain: Printing a single chip layer using two, three or four separate plates and etching steps, because one exposure cannot resolve features that close together. It is what a fab does when it cannot get sharper light.
why: China reaches advanced processes this way without extreme ultraviolet machines, taking roughly 34 lithography steps where nine would do, which is the direct source of its yield and cost penalty.

aka: process node, technology node, for example N2 or 18A
plain: The name a foundry gives one generation of its manufacturing process. The number in the name stopped measuring anything on the chip decades ago: nothing on TSMC's N2 is 2 nanometres wide, and SMIC's 5 nanometre-class process has a tighter metal spacing than Intel's 18A.
why: Because node names are marketing labels rather than measurements, rules and comparisons that lean on them are unreliable, which is why US export thresholds specify transistor type and metal spacing instead.

aka: GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72
plain: Nvidia's rack-sized product: 72 accelerators and 36 processors wired into one machine that software can treat as a single computer. The GB300 version draws up to 142 kilowatts.
why: AI capacity is now bought and priced by the rack, at roughly $5.0 million for a Grace Blackwell one and an estimated $7.8 million for its Vera Rubin successor.

plain: Nvidia's private high-speed connection between its own accelerators, carrying up to 3,600 gigabytes per second per chip so that dozens of them can act as one. No other vendor sells a switch with comparable bandwidth.
why: A genuine single-vendor chokepoint inside an otherwise competitive systems layer, and the reason the rest of the industry created the UALink standard to break it.

plain: A small device that turns electrical signals into laser light for sending down a glass fibre, and turns them back at the far end. Every network link longer than a few metres in a large AI cluster needs one at each end.
why: Chinese firms supply more than half the world's high-speed modules, and the indium phosphide lasers inside them ran at roughly half of demand in early 2026.

plain: A contract firm that takes finished wafers, cuts them into chips, seals the chips into packages and tests them. It is the back end of chipmaking, done for hire.
why: A low-margin business at 14 to 20 percent, with four of the ten largest firms Chinese and its tools largely outside the export control lines drawn around lithography and advanced deposition.

plain: How precisely one printed layer of a chip lands on top of the layer beneath it. The best machines hold this to under a nanometre, which is a few atoms of misalignment across a disc 300 millimetres wide.
why: Overlay is one of the specifications that separates an advanced printing machine from an ordinary one, and it gets worse every time a layer has to be printed in several passes.

plain: A thin transparent membrane held a few millimetres above a photomask so that dust settles on it rather than on the pattern, far enough out of focus that it does not print. It is a lens cap you can shoot through.
why: No membrane yet survives extreme ultraviolet light while passing enough of it, so fabs trade printing speed against defect risk product by product, and solving this would cut the cost of that printing more than any machine upgrade.

plain: A chip's TPP divided by the area of its logic dies in square millimetres, memory stacks excluded. It is a second test, not a replacement: it only applies to a chip that already reaches 1,600 TPP, and it catches parts that spread the same computing power over more silicon. It is the test that replaced the 2022 interconnect-bandwidth criterion.
why: It closed the gap the A800 and H800 used, and it is the clearest case of a control written as a formula rather than a product name. The threshold is 5.92 in ECCN 3A090.a (88 FR 73458).

plain: The master template for one layer of a chip: a quartz plate, or for the shortest wavelengths a mirror, carrying the pattern that gets projected onto the wafer. A leading-edge chip needs seventy to a hundred of them, and the full set costs $10 million to $40 million.
why: Mask cost decides which chips can afford a leading-edge process at all, and the blank plates the masks are made from come from just two Japanese suppliers.

plain: A liquid polymer spun onto a wafer in a film a few tens of nanometres thick that changes how easily it dissolves wherever light strikes it. Developing it, much like developing photographic film, washes away the exposed parts and leaves the printed pattern behind.
why: Japan supplies most of the world's photoresist, between 75 and 90 percent on published estimates, the largest maker is now owned outright by a Japanese state fund, and each resist is approved per layer per chip per fab so switching supplier takes years.

plain: A licence review policy, not a ban. An application may be filed and will be considered, but the reviewing agencies start from the position that it should be refused, and the exporter has to displace that. It is the policy for advanced computing chips going to China and Macau under 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10), and for most Entity List entries.
why: It is the distinction that decides whether a company files at all: under a presumption of denial an application can still be made, under a prohibition it cannot.

plain: A circuit board carrying thousands of fine needles that press down onto the contact pads of a chip while it is still part of the wafer, so a tester can drive signals into it. Every card is custom-built for one chip design.
why: Because cards are bespoke and slow to qualify, probe card supply and lead time gate how fast a new accelerator or memory stack can ramp to volume.

plain: The standard steel frame that computing equipment is bolted into in a data centre, roughly the size of a large refrigerator. AI systems have turned the rack from a container into the product, because an entire rack is now sold and wired as one machine.
why: Rack power went from about 120 kilowatts in 2024 to plans for a megawatt by 2027, and each step forces changes to cooling, busbars, floor loading and the substation outside.

plain: Shipping an item that is subject to the EAR from one foreign country to another, defined at 15 CFR 734.14. A Korean stack of memory moving from Korea to China is a reexport, and it needs the same US licence a shipment from Texas would.
why: Most of the trade the controls are aimed at never touches the United States. Without a hold on reexports the rules would only bind American ports.

plain: The patterned plate that a lithography machine projects onto the wafer, one chip layer at a time. In practice the word means the same as photomask, with reticle stressing that the machine steps the same image repeatedly across the disc.
why: The reticle's fixed printable area, 26 by 33 millimetres, is a hard physical limit that shapes how every large AI chip has to be designed.

plain: The largest chip a lithography machine can print in a single exposure, about 858 square millimetres, or 26 by 33 millimetres. It is set by the machine's optics, not by anything about the design.
why: Every AI accelerator worth buying is bigger than this, so designs must be split into chiplets and rejoined inside a package, which is how advanced packaging became the industry's bottleneck.

plain: The network that joins thousands of accelerator groups into one cluster, running at hundreds of gigabits per second over Ethernet or InfiniBand. The technology is ordinary data centre networking; the scale is not.
why: Ethernet has taken more than two thirds of this market from InfiniBand, which moved the value to merchant switch chips and to the optical modules that carry the traffic.

plain: The wiring that joins a few dozen accelerators inside one rack so a model too large for a single chip can be spread across them. It runs at terabytes per second, hundreds of times faster than the network between racks.
why: Scale-up bandwidth sets how large a model can be trained or served without choking, and Nvidia's NVLink is still the only product at the top of this market.

plain: The argument that Taiwan's dominance of advanced chipmaking deters an attack, because destroying or seizing TSMC would cost an aggressor and the world more than the island is worth.
why: The central and contested assumption behind Taiwan policy: a shield works only while it stays irreplaceable, which gives Taipei reason to slow the diversification its allies want.

plain: The stated design of US technology controls: restrict the narrow set of items that genuinely decide national security and leave the rest of the trade alone.
why: Whether the yard has stayed small is the standard test of whether export controls remain targeted security policy or have become general industrial policy.

plain: The test for whether an item falls under US export rules at all. Under 15 CFR 734.3 it covers anything in the United States, anything of US origin wherever it now sits, foreign-made goods that contain more than a permitted share of controlled US content, and foreign-made goods caught by a foreign direct product rule. Nationality of the seller is not the test; the item is.
why: The phrase decides who has to care. A Dutch or Korean firm shipping between two foreign countries can still need a US licence, because the item, not the exporter, is what the rules reach.

plain: The site's rating of how hard it would be for a well-funded state or firm, starting today, to stand up an alternative to the leaders of a stage, judged against four written tests. Easy: a qualified second source ships today at the leading node. Moderate: a second source exists but is not yet qualified at the leading node, about two to five years to close the gap. Hard: no second source at the leading node, five to ten years, and the path is known. Very hard: no second source, and the path runs through physics, decades of unwritten know-how or protected IP, ten years or more, and nobody has repeated it yet. The clock always times the same actor and runs to qualification, not to a prototype.
why: It is the one field on the card that rests on judgment rather than a count, so its four tests are spelled out above.

plain: The small, dense circuit board that a chip package sits on, spreading the chip's microscopic connections out to the millimetre-scale solder balls a motherboard can accept. It is built up layer by layer from epoxy film, laser-drilled holes and plated copper.
why: TSMC names substrates alongside memory as a limit on AI supply, and as packages grow, keeping a large one flat becomes harder than wiring it.

plain: The moment a chip design is declared finished and the pattern files are sent to the factory to be written into masks. The name survives from when the data physically left on a reel of magnetic tape.
why: After tape-out any change costs a new mask set and a new manufacturing run, so it is the point where hundreds of millions of dollars of downstream commitment becomes irreversible.

plain: The measure US export rules use for a chip's computing power: twice the number of multiply-accumulate operations it does each second, multiplied by the number of bits in each operation, added up across every processing unit on the chip. The definition sits in ECCN 3A090, in supplement no. 1 to 15 CFR part 774.
why: The dividing line for sales to China. Control starts at 4,800; since 15 January 2026 applications below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth are read case by case (91 FR 1685). Accelerators are now designed around the formula.

plain: Google's own AI chip, designed in-house rather than bought from Nvidia and used only inside Google's own data centres and cloud service. The seventh generation is called Ironwood.
why: The clearest evidence that a large buyer can build a real alternative to chips bought on the open market, with Google claiming a total cost per chip about 44 percent below that of the Nvidia server it replaces.

plain: The switch every chip is built from. Current runs through a channel between two terminals, and a voltage on a third terminal, the gate, opens or closes that path much as a tap opens or closes a pipe. One Nvidia Blackwell part contains 208 billion of them.
why: Everything in this supply chain exists to make transistors smaller, faster and less leaky, and the sheer difficulty of doing that is why the industry consolidated into so few firms.

plain: A copper column drilled all the way down through a chip so that power and signals can pass from its top face to its bottom face. It is what makes stacking chips vertically possible, in the way a lift shaft makes a tall building usable.
why: These columns are what make high bandwidth memory possible, and US rules control the tools that cut them by hole shape and etching speed.

plain: An authorisation BIS grants to a named foreign facility, letting approved items ship to it without an individual licence each time. The approved facilities are listed in supplement no. 7 to 15 CFR part 748, and the procedure is 15 CFR 748.15.
why: It is what let Intel, Samsung and SK hynix run their fabs inside China on general authority after 2022. Revoking it in 2025 did not stop those fabs; it made every shipment a licence application, and BIS said it would license operation but not expansion (90 FR 42321).

plain: The polished disc of ultrapure silicon that chips are built on, 300 millimetres across and less than a millimetre thick. Hundreds of chips are printed on one disc and cut apart at the end.
why: Five firms hold roughly 85 percent of 300 millimetre capacity, and this $11.4 billion market sits underneath trillions of dollars of downstream value.

plain: The collective name for the machines that process wafers inside a fab: printing systems, deposition and etch chambers, cleaning tools and measurement systems. It excludes the packaging and test machines used afterwards.
why: Spending on this equipment was a record $116.9 billion in 2025 and is the best early read on how much new chip capacity is being built, roughly two years before it produces anything.

plain: The percentage of chips on a wafer that work. Flaws land at random, so the larger the chip the more likely it is to catch one, and yield falls steeply as chips get bigger.
why: Yield, not wafer price, sets the cost of a working AI chip, and a ten point yield drop on a reticle-sized die hurts far more than a 30 percent rise in the wafer price.
